Prevention: Fusarium wilt is a fungi transmitted by seeds that cause wilt in tomato plants
Use non-infected clean seeds from healthy tomatoes, or certified clean seeds/ seedlings from authorized agro-dealer
Ensure machinery is cleaned with a 10 % chlorine bleach solution before being used in another field, or another area of the same field.
Also clean shoes and clothes after working if field is infected.
If soil is acidic, adjust soil pH to 6.5-7 using a nitrate (e.g. calcium nitrate) rather than using an ammonium nitrogen source, to reduce the incidence of disease
Dry weather and low soil moisture can encourage disease spread
However, avoid furrow and flood irrigation because water can move this disease (if using furrow irrigation ensure that water flows from fields not infected).
Keep the field clear of weeds since they can host the disease
Avoid damaging the roots of tomato plants.
The pathogen can enter through cuts and breaks
Control nematodes since they make resistant cultivars susceptible to the disease (see the 'Root knot nematodes on tomato' green list)
Carry out crop rotations of up to 5-7 years with non-susceptible crops such as wheat and rapeseed.
The pathogen can remain in the soil for years
After harvest, solarize the soil, leaving a clear plastic sheet on the soil surface for 4-6 weeks during the hottest part of the year.
This will help eliminating the fungi in the soil
Monitoring: Symptoms often appear later in the growing season and are first noticed on the lower (older) leaves
Leaves: yellowing and drooping of lower leaves, often occurring on one side of the plant or on one shoot.
Gradually more leaves yellow, wilt and die, usually before the plant reaches maturity
Whole plant: stunted growth and little or no fruit
To confirm for the disease, cut the stem and look for the presence of dark brown streaks running lengthwise through the stem
Consider taking control measures as soon as symptoms are noticed
Ensure that symptoms are caused by fusarium wilt and not bacterial wilt which induces similar symptoms.
Plants affected by bacterial wilt produce a milky exudate from stem pieces placed in water
Direct Control: Hand pull infected plants and destroy by burning (if allowed in your area).
Be sure to destroy/get rid of any plant residues so that they are not left to harbour and spread the disease.
Apply a heavy mulch to lower soil temperature and slow the growth of the pathogen
